quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

entry.rationale: The 1850 federal census is the first to name every member of a household with age and birthplace. Thomas and Sarah's household should list all children still at home, which tests for any child born before Mary (about 1836) or who died young. The 1830 and 1840 federal censuses name only the head, so they cannot list the children and are not planned for that purpose. Collection: United States Census, 1850, name-searchable.

The 1860 census names each household member with age and birthplace. It shows children born after 1850 (the tree's youngest, Joseph, is about 13 in 1860) and any child who was at home in 1850 but had left. Collection: United States Census, 1860, name-searchable.

Thomas died in 1868 according to the tree's death fact in Greene County. The 1870 census shows whether Sarah is now a widow heading her own household and which children, including any born after 1860, were still with her. Collection: United States Census, 1870, name-searchable.

The 1880 census gives relationship to head and birthplace for every member. It catches children born late in Sarah's child-bearing years who were still at home after 1870, and any widowed household that persisted. Collection: United States Census, 1880, name-searchable.

Baptism or christening entries name both parents and the child, and can show children who died before any census. The tree's births (Mary about 1836 through Joseph about 1847) are all placed in Greene County, so the baptism search is run there. Collection: Ohio, Births and Christenings, 1821-1962, name-searchable.

County birth registrations name the parents of each child. Coverage before statewide registration is uncertain, so any hit is a lead to verify against the original register, not proof. Collection: Ohio, County Births, 1841-2003, name-searchable.

The marriage of Thomas Hale and Sarah bounds the start of the child-bearing years: no child should be born before it, and a record may give Sarah's maiden surname and her parents' names. Greene County marriage records survive from 1803 per the locality entry. Collection: Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016, name-searchable.

Thomas's death in 1868 and Sarah's later death or burial can name survivors or give a household list. A death or burial entry may name the surviving children or the couple's ages. Collections: Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997, name-searchable.

Thomas's estate file, held by the Greene County Probate Court (the Court of Common Pleas handled probate until 1852), would name heirs and may list the children, and any guardianship for minors after Sarah's death would name the children as wards. This is browse-only: the Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996 collection is browse-only, so the item is an image browse of the Greene County dockets, not a name search.

Surrounding-family item: each known child's marriage record, when found, names the bride or groom's parents, and a sibling's marriage can name the same parents. Marriage bondsmen and witnesses are also associates who may be siblings or other kin. Run once for each of Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph. Collection: Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016, name-searchable.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Her maiden name comes from this marriage only if it was her first. Pennsylvania Church Marriages, 1682-1976 and Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 are both name-searchable for the county. A nil result does not rule out an Irish marriage, which needs a locality survey for Ireland before it can be planned.

Sibling baptisms: Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 is name-searchable. Searching for children with Thomas Flynn as father, born in the county after Patrick, tests for siblings. A baptism names the mother and so supplies her maiden name, which neither the 1850 nor the 1860 census household gives. A sibling entry naming the same father is also the first record that places Patrick and another child with both parents.

Thomas Flynn's estate: Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county Register of Wills files, not a name search. The window runs from Patrick's birth to about age 87 for Thomas, who was born ca. 1818, since a probate file can be filed decades after the events it records. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence and could also name the wife and other children. The county was formed in 1811, so its probate files are available for this period.

Thomas Flynn's burial and death entry: Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 and Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 are both name-searchable. A burial entry often gives age, birthplace and a spouse's name. The 1850-1880 Mortality Schedules, a national name-searchable collection, can also show whether he died in the county in those years. Pennsylvania statewide death registration began only in 1906, so before then this route depends on church and cemetery entries.

The 1880 census is the one household schedule that states each person's relationship to the head. The proof summary names it as a gap, with 1870 and 1900 also unsearched, and it is the record that would move the 1850 and 1860 inferences from indirect to direct. United States, Census, 1880 is name-searchable. Searching Thomas Flynn's household for Patrick as son would close the relationship question without needing a church record.

Patrick Flynn's own estate, filed after his death on 12 March 1908: Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only. A file for a man who died in 1908 names his heirs, which can identify siblings and possibly the mother. The window is sized to the filing period after the death, not to the 1845-1908 research window.

Family, neighbour and associate (FAN) item: the marriage of James Brown, who gave the 1908 death certificate's parentage as son-in-law, to a daughter of Patrick Flynn. Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 is name-searchable. A bride's marriage record normally names her father, which would confirm Patrick's own parentage through his child, and it may name Brown's witnesses and bondsmen, who could be further relatives. It is a lead for the parentage question, not evidence of it.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tests the family tradition of coal mining directly: the 1880 census records each man's occupation, so Michael's entry should read miner or similar, along with his household. It also shows whether he lived in the household of his brother Patrick Sheahan (I2), who was already in Schuylkill County by 1875 per the tree's residence fact and deed, which would make kin already in the county the likely draw. Name-searchable (United States, Census, 1880). Log_002 places him there in 1882 only, so this is the first check of the move's timing.

Tests whether Michael bought land or took a lease in the county before or around 1882. Coal-region land was often leased from mining companies rather than purchased, so a lease or a lease-linked deed is as informative as a purchase. The image group is browse-only (volume_search shows about 22 percent record-searchable), so it is read page by page in the Recorder of Deeds index for Sheahan entries. The same browse covers Patrick Sheahan's 1875 purchase from James Kelly (S2), a FAN check on whether the brothers acquired property together.

Pennsylvania Church Marriages is name-searchable. Michael's marriage, if it took place in the county around 1882, would give his residence and occupation at the time and could show the move was made with a wife or to join a settled family. A marriage in the 1870s elsewhere would instead date the move earlier. Records here are kept at the parish or diocese for Roman Catholic marriages, so a county-level name search may miss them; the browse item below covers that gap.

Fallback for the church-marriage name search. The marriage register image group for the county is browse-only (volume_search shows no record-searchable content), so it is read image by image for Michael's marriage entry, with residence and occupation of the groom. Used only if the name search returns nothing.

Church registers for the county are browse-only. Baptism entries for Michael's children born in the county would give his residence and occupation at the time of each baptism, placing him in the county by a fixed date. Roman Catholic registers are held at the parish or the Diocese of Philadelphia, which covered Schuylkill in this period, so the browse should be matched to parish records and not treated as the only register.

If Michael was foreign-born, a naturalization declaration or petition filed in the county would give his country of origin, arrival date and the residence he gave when he filed. The collection runs past the window, and declarations were often filed years after arrival, so the item is sized to the collection's own span rather than cut to 1882. The image group is browse-only, so the court index is read page by page. His birthplace is not recorded in the tree, so this item tests whether he was an immigrant at all.

Michael's death or burial entry, if he died in the county, would name his residence, occupation and sometimes his birthplace, which is the usual route to an origin the tree does not record. The tree gives no death date for him, so this is searched by name for the years after his 1882 residence. Name-searchable (Pennsylvania Cemetery Records and Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials).

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?
items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

items.notes: Found Patrick Flynn age 5 in household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, Schuylkill Co. Three other Flynn results examined — ages and locations don't match.
Ancestry index confirms same household. Transcription matches FamilySearch except Ancestry reads dwelling as 84, FamilySearch as 84 — consistent.
MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.
Patrick Flynn age 15 in household of Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill Co. Consistent with 1850 placement.
Death certificate found. Names Thomas Flynn as father. Informant was son-in-law James Brown.

entry.rationale: The 1850 (log_001) and 1860 (log_004) censuses place Patrick Flynn in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County, so this 1880 census tests whether the pair still shared a dwelling as Patrick reached adulthood. Thomas (tree birth about 1818, Ireland) would be about 62 and Patrick about 35. The 1880 census is the first federal census to record relationship to head of household, so it can show Patrick as Thomas's son directly. The national census collection is name-searchable. The tree gives Patrick's birth as Ireland, while the earlier searches used Pennsylvania as birthplace, so search without a birthplace filter.

The 1870 census falls between the 1860 entry (Patrick age 15, log_004) and adulthood. Patrick would be about 25 and Thomas about 52. The 1870 schedule does not record relationship to head, so a match must rest on co-residence, the Thomas Flynn name and an Irish birthplace, with ages compared against the 1860 entry. The national census collection is name-searchable. If Thomas appears in a separate household, that weighs against the placement but does not disprove parentage.

By 1900 Patrick (about 55) is likely the head of his own household, and Thomas (about 82 if living) probably is not in it. The 1900 schedule records relationship to head, birth month and year, and each parent's birthplace, so a Thomas listed as father-in-law or parent would be direct evidence. The national census collection is name-searchable. Absence of Thomas here does not show Thomas was not Patrick's father, since he may have died before 1900.

Fan item. The death certificate (log_005) names son-in-law James Brown as informant, so Brown married a daughter of Patrick, and that daughter's household would be a Flynn family unit. Search the 1880 Schuylkill household of James Brown, which may be too early to hold Patrick's daughter, for any Flynn or Thomas Flynn living with the Browns or a neighbour. Brown is a common name, so match on the Brown household's full composition and the Schuylkill location, not on the name alone. The national census collection is name-searchable.

Parents' marriage item. A marriage of Thomas Flynn (tree birth about 1818) to Patrick's mother is needed to confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's maiden name, and date the union before Patrick's birth about 1845. The date window is sized to Thomas's plausible marriage age and Patrick's birth. If the marriage took place in Ireland, no Pennsylvania record will exist, so a miss here is not decisive. Search the Pennsylvania county marriage and church marriage collections, and check for a remarriage if the wife's name changes between records.

Run first because the mother's name is needed for the marriage and baptism searches that follow.

Tree fact F2 records Patrick Flynn's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, so the 1910 household should be his widow's, with Margaret about thirteen. The United States Census, 1910 is name-searchable. It gives Margaret's birth year again and tests whether the head or wife is the same woman named in 1900.

Marriage of Patrick Flynn to Margaret's mother before her birth. The County Marriages and Civil Marriages collections are name-searchable. The record names the bride, which supplies the mother's name for the baptism search. Patrick was about 52 at Margaret's birth, so search for any earlier marriage too; if the bride here was not Margaret's mother, a second marriage is the likely reason.

A Catholic baptism is the likely source of Margaret's birth date. Pennsylvania statewide birth registration began in 1906, after her birth, so the birth certificate route is closed. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable. Search Margaret Flynn with Patrick Flynn as father. The sacramental register is held at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, so the indexed entry may be a transcription; confirm against the image where one is available.

The locality guide records that the Schuylkill County Orphans' Court kept registers of births from 1893 to 1905, which covers Margaret's birth about 1897. Access is unknown and no name index was returned, so this is a browse of the register by year. It gives a birth date and parents' names independent of the church.

Fallback for the baptism search. If no baptism is found, a delayed birth registration may state the date. The Pennsylvania Delayed Birth Records collection is name-searchable and runs to 1977, so the item is sized to that span, since delayed filings were made long after the event.

FAN item. Sibling baptisms of Patrick Flynn's children name the same parents and give the spacing of the births, which bears on Margaret's date. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable. Search Flynn children with Patrick as father, and then with the mother's name once item 3 supplies it.

Patrick Flynn died in 1908, so his estate file was made after that death. The window is sized to his death and the settling of heirs, not to Margaret's birth. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse at the Schuylkill County Register of Wills. An estate file may list minor heirs with their ages or dates of birth.

Margaret's own marriage record, if she married. The County Marriages and Civil Marriages collections are name-searchable. A bride's record gives her age and her parents' names, which confirm the birth date. Match on Patrick Flynn and the mother's name, since Flynn is a common surname.

Margaret's own death or burial entry. Her birth falls before the 1906 statewide register, so a death or burial that states her age or date of birth is a route to the birth date. The Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records collections are name-searchable. Use the same surname-and-parent check as item 9.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Fills the 1851-1860 gap in the timeline (t_001). Patrick, age 5 in 1850, would be about 15. The 1850 co-residence in Thomas Flynn's dwelling 84 was searched under pl_001 for q_002 (log_001 to log_003) and shows only a household link. The 1860 census does not state relationships, so this item tests whether Thomas Flynn still heads a household that includes a Patrick of the right age. Name-searchable (United States, Census, 1860).

Tests the Thomas Flynn household again in 1870, when Patrick would be about 25 and Thomas about 52 if both lived. The 1870 census records each person's birthplace, which bears on the conflict between the tree (F1 and a_002 give Ireland) and the objective (born in Pennsylvania). It does not state relationships. Name-searchable (United States, Census, 1870).

The 1880 census is the first US census to state each person's relationship to the head of household. A Patrick recorded as son of Thomas Flynn would be the first record in the project that names the relationship directly, replacing the inferred child relationship in a_004, which rests only on household position and shared surname. Name-searchable (United States, Census, 1880).

Parents' marriage search for Thomas Flynn (born about 1818 per tree fact F3), with any wife, keyed on the groom's surname because no wife is named anywhere in the project. The window is set by Thomas's age at a first marriage (about 18 at the earliest, so about 1836) and by Patrick's birth about 1845. Schuylkill County was formed in 1811, so no parent-county split applies. Pennsylvania County Marriages 1775-1991 is name-searchable. The record supplies a mother's maiden name only if that marriage was her first, which is not yet known, so no maiden name is assumed; a second marriage would appear under another surname. The marriage alone does not establish Patrick as their child; that needs a record placing him with them. If the couple married in Ireland before emigrating, this item will not find it, and an Irish search needs a locality survey first.

Fallback for the county marriage search. Pennsylvania Church Marriages 1682-1976 is name-searchable and holds Catholic marriages that a county index may omit. Catholic sacramental registers are kept at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county, and Schuylkill stayed with Philadelphia until 1961 (loc_001 quirk), so the search runs by surname across the county and any parish named in the results.

entry.repository: Schuylkill County Register of Wills (FamilySearch images)
entry.rationale: Tests whether Thomas Flynn left a will or an administration naming a son Patrick, which would be direct parentage evidence. The window is set by Thomas's lifespan (born about 1818 per F3), not by Patrick's: a will could fall anywhere from the 1850s to about 1900, when Thomas would be about 82. The Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811 (loc_001). quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: The 1850 and 1860 censuses place Patrick in Thomas Flynn's household but state no relationships (log_001, log_004; ps_001). The 1880 census is the first to record each person's relationship to the head, so it is the direct test of whether Patrick is Thomas's son. The US 1880 census is name-searchable.

The 1870 census is the one decennial gap in the household series (ps_001 lists it as unsearched). It shows whether the Thomas Flynn household and Patrick persisted between 1860 and 1880. It records no relationships, so it corroborates continuity rather than parentage. The US 1870 census is name-searchable.

The 1900 census records relationship to the head and is the last census before Patrick's 1908 death (ps_001 lists it as unsearched). If Thomas (born about 1818) was still living, a 1900 household with Patrick as son tests parentage again. The US 1900 census is name-searchable.

Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother. Its date relative to Patrick's birth (about 1845) corroborates Thomas as father and supplies the mother's maiden name, which the census and death certificate omit. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Pennsylvania, County Marriages (1775-1991) is name-searchable. Civil registration was not statewide until 1906, so this is a county record.

A separate search for the Catholic marriage of Thomas Flynn, which the county record may not hold. Pennsylvania, Church Marriages (1682-1976) is name-searchable. Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia, so sacramental registers sit at the parish or diocese, not the county. The entry may name the bride's parents or her maiden name, and it can show a remarriage.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration, held by the county Register of Wills (county formed 1811; ps_001 names this as the primary gap). The window runs from Patrick's birth to about age 82 for Thomas, because Thomas was born about 1818 and his death date is unknown. A will naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of parentage. The Pennsylvania, Probate Records (1683-1994) collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county dockets, not a name search.

Friends and family of the parents (FAN). Baptisms of Patrick's siblings, or marriages of his sisters or brothers, that name Thomas Flynn as father would confirm the household as a family unit. Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings (1709-1950) and County Marriages are name-searchable. Their records may name the same parents, and that test is independent of the census household.

Patrick's burial entry, dated to his 1908 death. Burial entries often state age, birthplace, or a parent's name, and this would check the death certificate's Pennsylvania birthplace against the census's Ireland. Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records (1700-1950) is name-searchable.

## Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain — 1835-1870

Before civil registration (1871) the parish books are the vital record. Santa María's books from 1837 are on FamilySearch, unindexed but full-text searchable; one births volume for 1841-1845 is name-indexed.

entry.rationale: Subject is recorded as born about 1843 in Vélez-Málaga. Before civil registration (1871) the parish baptism register is the primary record (loc_001). The 1841-1845 births volume (image group 004458370) is 96% name-searchable, and Spain, Baptisms (collection 1500692) is name-searchable at collection level. Baptism entries of this period normally name both parents and the four grandparents, so this is the most likely single record to answer the question. Search for María Josefa with García and Romero as the name.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain
entry.rationale: Dedicated parents' marriage item. The couple's marriage confirms them as a unit, dates their union against the 1843 birth, and, if it was the mother's first marriage, supplies her maiden name, which the baptism may give only as a surname. Search Spain, Marriages (collection 1500693, name-searchable) and the religious marriage coverage of 004104131_001 (1837-1895, full-text). Per Spain Naming Customs a woman keeps her maiden surname on marriage, so the bride's record should carry Romero. The marriage on its own does not prove this child is theirs; that needs the baptism (items 1-2).

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain
entry.rationale: Fan item for a parentage question: full-text co-occurrence search on García and Romero as two separate terms across image groups 004104131_001 and 004104131_002, to find the parents' other acts. Later children's baptisms, a sibling's marriage or a godparent entry names the same parents and bears on whether the candidate couple is the right one. Per Spain Naming Customs the first surname is the father's and the second the mother's, so García is the presumed father's surname and Romero the mother's; this is a reading to test, not a settled fact, and the search keeps both orders open.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain
entry.rationale: Companion to item 3: test whether the mother named Romero had an earlier marriage. Spanish women keep their maiden surname, but a record of a later household or a prior marriage can name her under another surname, so the surname on one marriage record does not settle her first marriage. Full-text search the religious marriage coverage of 004104131_001 and 004104131_002, and Spain, Marriages (1500693), for a Romero bride marrying in 1830-1843 with a different groom.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain
entry.rationale: Find the father's death or burial and test whether a widowed mother remarried (item 5). The window is sized to the father's plausible lifespan: a father active at the 1843 birth, born roughly 1800-1820, could die as late as 1870. Full-text search 004104131_001 religious death records and, at collection level, Spain, Deaths (1500694, name-searchable), for a García who died in Vélez-Málaga.

Contingent item: if the father died while the child was young, a Vélez-Málaga orphan admission would name the child and usually the deceased parent. Image group 008216391_001 (orphans and orphanages, 1815-1911) is browse-only and not name-searchable, so this is an image browse. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.rationale: Primary research objective. The subject's patronymic 'Nielsen' implies a father named Niels, but no father is identified in the tree and no records have been searched yet.

entry.rationale: Denmark Military Levying Rolls (laegdsruller) enrol every Danish boy from birth under his father's name, so a roll entry for Mikkel's boyhood would name his father directly. Mikkel was born 20 Aug 1779, so the first roll that lists him is from 1789, when he was about ten. The collection is name-searchable, so search Mikkel Nielsen with a 1779 birth year and a Stagstrup link. The date range runs to the collection's own last year, 1861, because a man stayed on the roll until age 34 and later rolls can still name a father. The Stagstrup link is what the locality survey gives for the parish; the rolls are organized by Thisted Amt districts.

Browse fallback for the levy-roll name search. The image group covers the Thisted Amt district rolls for 1789-1814 and is browse-only, so read the Stagstrup district pages by hand for the Mikkel Nielsen entry under his father's name. Use it if the name search returns nothing or only partial matches. A roll naming a boy under his father is direct parentage evidence.

The baptism of Mikkel, born 20 Aug 1779, should fall in late August 1779. The Stagstrup church book is in range (the register covers 1763-1814), so a baptism exists and the birth window is not out of reach. Denmark's baptism entries name both parents, so this entry can give the father's name directly. Search the name-indexed Church Books collection first, though the Stagstrup register is only thinly indexed, so the image browse in the next item is the main route. Naming customs apply: Danish first sons were often named for the father's father, and second sons for the mother's father, so Mikkel may be named for his maternal grandfather. A given name in the entry is not proof of the father's name by itself.

Browse the Stagstrup kirkebog image group for the 1779 baptisms, page by page, for the entry dated late August 1779 for Mikkel. This is the fallback for the baptism name search, since the register's index is thin. The image group is browse-only. The entry names the father and the mother, and it also names the godparents (used in a later item). Verify the father's name against the entry itself, not an index.

Parents' marriage. Mikkel's father must have married before August 1779, so browse the Stagstrup marriage entries of about 1763-1779 for a Niels who married a woman who then bore children in the parish. The entry supplies the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage. We do not yet know whether she married before, so treat her maiden name as unsettled. This marriage entry corroborates a father named by other evidence, but it does not by itself show Mikkel is their child; that needs the baptism or a census that places him with the parents.

Denmark Census 1787 is name-searchable and falls when Mikkel was about seven, so it can place him in a Stagstrup household with a male head. If a Niels heads a household listing a boy named Mikkel, that links the father to the child directly. If no Niels is found, the census may show a widow or another household head who is the mother's household. Search by the subject's name and the parish.

Denmark Census 1801 is name-searchable and falls when Mikkel was about 21. If he is still in the parental household, the schedule places him with the head of household, and the head's name is the father if the father was alive in 1801. If the father is absent, the census shows whether the head is a widow, which tests whether the father had died by then. This item tests whether the father was alive and whether Mikkel was in his household.

A probate index entry for a Niels of Stagstrup would give the father's death and name the children in his estate division. The date window is sized to the father's lifespan, not to Mikkel's. A father of a child born in 1779 was probably born about 1735-1755 and could have died anywhere from 1779 to about 1815, so the window runs to 1840. The Probate Indexes collection is name-searchable. Confirm the parish falls in Hassing Herred before relying on the herred-level record.

Browse fallback for the probate name search. The Hassing Herred probate volume (skifteprotokoller) is browse-only, so read the Stagstrup estate divisions by hand for the father's estate and its heirs. Use it if the index yields no Niels of Stagstrup. The date window is sized to the father's likely lifespan, as in the previous item.

FAN item. The godparents and any witnesses named in Mikkel's baptism entry (found in the item above) are often kin or close neighbours, and sponsors were often chosen from the father's or mother's family. Once the baptism entry is read, search the Stagstrup records for each sponsor's own baptisms, marriages and levy entries to see whether they carry the father's name or a family link. Any sponsor who turns out to be the father's brother or the mother's kin is a lead to the father's identity.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZWK-EL1 before searching; an attached hint may already answer the question.

Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 (collection 1417491) is name-searchable and is the only statewide death certificate series. The tree holds no death fact, so a certificate can answer the question only if Elijah died on or after 1 January 1911; a death in the 1870s-1880s cannot have a certificate here. Search by name with Muhlenberg County as place and the death year open, then read the certificate for date, place and informant, and test identity against the 1870 Muhlenberg residence fact in the tree.

Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (collection 1804888, name-searchable) holds county death registers for 1852-1910, where coverage for the 1860s-1870s is partial. This is the only register form that can record a pre-1911 death, so it covers the period the 1870 residence leaves open. A negative search does not prove absence, since many counties have no surviving register for those decades.

Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 (collection 1875188) is browse-only, so this is an image browse of Muhlenberg County probate volumes, not a name search. Administrator bonds name the widow or adult son, and estate settlements are dated, so they bracket a pre-1911 death within months and localize it to the county. Probate is the primary death evidence for this era, since no certificate can cover it.

The 1870 residence in Muhlenberg County is the last trace in the tree. A 1880 United States census household for Elijah, name-searchable, would show whether he was alive and at home that year, which narrows the death window to 1870-1880 or later. Its neighbours also serve as FAN leads. Search by name and age near 1814 in Muhlenberg County.

Kentucky County Marriages, 1797-1954 (collection 1804987, name-searchable) is the FAN item for the identity question. Elijah's own marriage names his wife, who may later be the estate administrator, and the bondsman, often a brother-in-law or kinsman, who can confirm the family. It also dates his first marriage, which bounds the probate search.

Church burial registers and county cemetery records can bracket the death when no certificate or probate file survives. Search the Muhlenberg County cemetery and church burial lists for Elijah Wilkins with a burial date and a stated age that fits a birth near 1814. A grave record is secondary evidence and must be checked against the original register.

items.guide_markdown:
## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

entry.jurisdiction: Lincolnshire, England (parish of baptism, not yet identified)
entry.rationale: Mary Dawson's christening should name her father and mother. Born about 1772, so the baptism window is 1766-1778. Search the name-searchable FamilySearch collection 'England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975' (loc_001, collection 1473014). The locality guide marks it a partial Legacy index, so a nil result shows only what the index holds, not that no christening exists. The collection search returned no Lincolnshire rows this session, so the collection is cited from loc_001. The place name did not resolve in place_search, so the jurisdiction is written as the locality entry names it.

entry.jurisdiction: Lincolnshire, England (parish of baptism, not yet identified)
entry.rationale: Fallback for item 1. If the partial index returns nothing, browse the parish baptism register page by page once the parish is identified. The locality guide says absence from the index is not proof of absence, so the register itself must be checked. volume_search returned no volume for this place this session, so locate the register through the FamilySearch Catalog before browsing.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, kept separate from the baptism search. Its rationale: it confirms the couple as a unit, and if it is the mother's first marriage it supplies her maiden name, which census and burial records often omit. Its date set against the 1772 birth corroborates a father named only indirectly, but it does not by itself prove Mary is their child. Mary's baptism or a record placing her with both parents is still needed. Search keyed on the surname Dawson, since the mother's name is unknown. Companion check: the mother may have married more than once, so also search for any other marriage of a Dawson woman in the same parishes, and do not treat the first marriage found as hers by default.

FAN item for the Dawson household. Search baptisms of other Dawson children in Lincolnshire, 1766-1790, that name the same parents, since a sibling's christening can name the parents when Mary's own entry is missing or unreadable. Also search godparent and witness names on those entries. These are associates whose records may bear on the question. The survey found no record of other children for Mary, so every sibling candidate remains unverified.

entry.jurisdiction: Lincolnshire, England (parish of Mary's marriage, not yet identified)
entry.rationale: Mary's own marriage record, planned because the birth register may not reach back to 1772 in her parish (register start date not yet established in the locality entry). Marriage entries and marriage bonds or licences often name the bride's father and her parish of residence. Search keyed on her name Mary Dawson; if she married under a later surname, the search will not match, so use it as a check, not a gate.

entry.jurisdiction: Lincolnshire, England (parish of last residence, not yet identified)
entry.rationale: Mary's own burial or death entry. A burial register usually gives an age, which fixes the birth year, and sometimes a parish or father's name. This is a route to her origin if the baptism register does not survive or is not in the index. Dated after her birth window and set in the parish where she last lived. Search keyed on Mary Dawson. Her death is not yet recorded in the tree, so this is planned as a route to origin, not a confirmed death.

entry.jurisdiction: Lincolnshire, England (diocese and archdeaconry courts covering the parish, to be identified)

## Württemberg, Germany - 1780-1830

German children baptised with two or more given names were often called by the second in daily life (the wiki's example: Johann Christoph and Johann Friedrich were usually called Christoph and Friedrich) — search later records under the second given name alone as well as the full baptismal name. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs)

entry.rationale: Anna Margaretha Bauer's baptism (birth 1792, Württemberg) is the most direct route to naming her parents. The locality entry lists Germany, Births and Baptisms, 1558-1898 (collection 1473000), which is name-searchable: search surname Bauer with given name Anna, and also under Margaretha, because the locality quirk says the second given name was often the one used in daily life. The locality entry records no register start date for her parish, so the baptism may be missing; if the search fails, the sibling and marriage items carry the search forward.

FAN item, required on a parentage question. Baptisms of Bauer siblings in the same parish (collection 1473000, name-searchable) name the same parents as Anna's own baptism would. Search Bauer baptisms in the years around 1792 and note any child whose parents match. This is useful if Anna's baptism is missing or illegible, and it tests whether the family is the one assumed.

Parents' marriage record, kept separate from the baptism item. Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (collection 1473009, name-searchable) may show the couple as a unit and, if this was the mother's first marriage, give her maiden name. Because her remarriage is unknown, plan the search on the surname this record gives her and, separately, for any second marriage of the mother, since a later marriage can give a different surname. A marriage date before 1792 supports the father of a child born in 1792; it does not by itself prove the child is theirs.

## Locality Guide: Trysil, Hedmark, Norway (1780–1880)

### Jurisdictional Context

Trysil became its own *prestegjeld* in 1780, separated from Elverum. The 1860 death falls squarely within Trysil's own records. Administratively: Amt of Hedmark from 1781; Sorenskriveri of Søndre Østerdalen; Diocese of Oslo/Christiania 1537–1864, then Hamar.

### Church Records — Primary Source

- **Digitized images** (browse-only, 0% name-indexed): Kirkebøker 1588–1928 (Trysil prestegjeld) at FamilySearch Catalog (cat. 737) and Digitalarkivet. The 1860 burial will be in volume 008679203_003 (1814–1877, 325 images).
- **Indexed national extracts** (name-searchable): Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081; also Ancestry, MyHeritage); Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014); Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080).
- **Dissenter church**: Trysil Frimenighet 1858–1920 at Digitalarkivet (images).

### Census

| Year | FS Collection | Access | Notes |
|------|--------------|--------|-------|
| 1801 | 3733603 | indexed & images | Subject ~21; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |
| 1865 | 3756102 | indexed & images | Postdates death; shows widow/children |
| 1870 | 4135961 | indexed & images | Postdates death |
| 1875 | 1529106 | indexed & images | Postdates death; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |

### Probate

- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306): indexed — locate the 1860 estate filing here.
- Skifteprotokoller image volumes at FS Catalog cover through 1853; post-1853 volumes held at Riksarkivet/Digitalarkivet.

### Land Records

- Pantebøker (mortgage/property) 1712–1860 (FS Catalog 489152) — images.

### Military / Levy Rolls

Norway's conscription/levy rolls (*lægdsruller*) began 1789. Each enrolled boy is listed under his father's name — direct parentage evidence. A male born ~1780 would appear from approximately 1789. Access via Riksarkivet and Digitalarkivet.

### Farm Books (*Bygdebøker*)

Trysilboka (Lillevold, Larsen, Bryn; FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l) — multiple volumes covering farm histories and resident genealogies for Trysil with personal name indexes in volumes 1–3, 7–8. High-value source for locating a household at the farm level.

### Key Access Points

- **FamilySearch** (free): indexed burials/baptisms/marriages/census, browse church record images
- **Digitalarkivet** (free): church books at media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse
- **Ancestry** (subscription): Norway Burials/Baptisms/Marriages extracts, 1865 census
- **MyHeritage** (subscription): Norway Burials/Marriages, 1865/1875 census
- **FamilySearch Library** (on-site or center): Trysilboka farm book, catalog microfilm

## Kongsberg Parish, Buskerud, Norway — Locality Guide (1760–1810)

**Ecclesiastical jurisdiction:** Kongsberg prestegjeld, Kongsberg prosti, Oslo bispedømme (until 1948). Civil jurisdiction in 1780: Buskerud amt (from 1680), Numedal og Sandsvær sorenskriveri, Kongsberg Byfogderi (probate/skifterett).

### Church Records

All Kongsberg church record volumes at FamilySearch are **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Browse image by image.

**Key FamilySearch volumes for a ~1780 baptism:**
- **008680156_003** (1769–1782, 382 images) — prime target for a ~1780 birth
- **008680157_002** (1783–1797, 249 images) — wider date window fallback
- **008680157_003** (1795–1816, 380 images)
- **009061212** (Kongsberg + Jondalen combined, 1696–1915, 691 images)

**National indexed extracts (searchable):**
- Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014): 28,370 Kongsberg records — search first; coverage of 1780s may be incomplete
- Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080)
- Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081)
- Same extracts also at Ancestry (Norway Select Baptisms col 60092) and MyHeritage

**Digitalarkivet:** Complete parish register scans 1696–1969 at media.digitalarkivet.no (Buskerud county, Kongsberg prestegjeld). Both Kongsberg proper and Jondalen sub-parish registers are available. Same material as FS volumes; browse by year range.

### Census Records
- 1801 census (FS col 3733603, indexed + images; also Digitalarkivet, Ancestry, MyHeritage)
- No pre-1801 national census; the mine rolls below partially fill this gap

### Kongsberg Sølvverk (Silver Mine) Records
Special census-type rolls at Digitalarkivet for mine employees:
- Pensjonister (pensioners) 1711; Borgere (citizens/residents) 1723; Funksjonærer (officials) 1765
These predate the ~1780 birth but may document a father employed at the mine.

### Military / Conscription (Lægdsruller)
Norwegian levy rolls began 1789. A male born ~1780 enrolled ~age 7–9, listed directly **under his father's name** — direct parentage evidence. Access: Digitalarkivet (browse and search) and Riksarkivet physical holdings for Numedal og Sandsvær lægd.

### Probate Records
- Kongsberg Byfogderi Skifteprotokoller 1739–1851 (FS Catalog 437559, browse-only; also Digitalarkivet)
- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306, indexed)
- Kongsberg deanery probate 1741–1816 at Digitalarkivet

### Land and Property
- Pantebøker (mortgage books) 1721–1864 at FamilySearch Catalog (no. 485469, Kongsberg Byfogderi)

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.
